title: An Execution‑Oriented Evaluation of Generate→Validate→Simulate→Rollback Pipelines for LLM‑Assisted NetOps: a Confirmatory Study with gpt‑5‑mini
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory comparison of (A) a generation‑only pipeline and (C) a generate→validate→simulate→rollback (guarded) pipeline for LLM‑assisted NetOps configuration tasks. Using gpt‑5‑mini under a frozen design (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (routing, ACL, NAT), the deterministic simulator adjudicated an actionable‑misconfiguration binary per task. Results: baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160; paired difference = 0.00, 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729); McNemar exact p = 1.00. The preregistered target (≥30% relative reduction) cannot be evaluated because the baseline actionable rate was zero (ceiling effect). We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, raw outputs, scoring artifacts, and analysis traces (paths and hashes recorded in the execution manifest). We discuss construct and external validity, limitations, and concrete directions for harder task sets, multi‑model evaluation, and richer validators.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are proposed to accelerate NetOps tasks (intent→configuration, change planning, limited self‑healing) but pose operational risks when outputs are enacted [Khurshid et al., VeriFlow 2012; Mondal et al. 2023; Zhou et al. 2025]. Prior work advocates generate→validate→repair architectures but lacks fully preregistered execution evidence that ties model generation to deterministic enactment outcomes. We ask a narrowly scoped confirmatory question (preregistered id c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1): does pipeline C (generate→validate→simulate→rollback) reduce the actionable misconfiguration rate by ≥30% relative to a generation‑only baseline (A)? We contribute a fully preregistered, artifacted, paired execution using gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic simulator adjudication, and complete audit traces.
sections.related_work: This study sits at the intersection of (i) network verification and incremental update checking (VeriFlow and follow‑on verifiers), (ii) LLM→NetOps generation with constraint/validator augmentation (e.g., Verified Prompt Programming, MeshAgent), and (iii) Ops/AIOps benchmarking efforts that emphasize operational enactment (OpsEval family). Unlike capability benchmarks that evaluate text correctness, we measure enactability via a deterministic simulator and a preregistered paired hypothesis test. We cite representative closest works in the execution manifest and preregistration (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology: Preregistration: the full experimental plan (c1_exec_benchmark_2026_prereg_v1) froze design, seeds, selection, metrics, stopping rules, retry policy, and analysis before execution (manifested in execution_manifest). Design: paired confirmatory comparison (baseline A vs guarded C) on N=160 vendor‑neutral tasks (approx. routing 64, ACL 64, NAT/other 32). Model and prompting: single hosted model gpt‑5‑mini; one shared initial generation call per task; up to one repair call pre‑registered (not needed in confirmatory set). Guarded pipeline: generation → constraint/validator → deterministic simulator enactment → automatic rollback scoring. Baseline: same generation prompt, simulator scoring of generated config but no in‑pipeline pre‑enactment validation. Primary metric: per‑task binary actionable misconfiguration label from deterministic simulator. Primary estimand: paired difference in actionable proportion (A − C). Analysis: paired bootstrap (10k replicates, seed=1729) for CI and McNemar exact test for paired binary outcome. Reproducibility: all prompts, seeds, canonicalizers, simulator, raw outputs, scoring JSONs, and analysis scripts archived; artifact paths/hashes in execution_manifest and analysis artifacts (see execution_manifest.artifact_hashes and analysis artifact hashes).
sections.results: Execution and raw artifacts: the run completed as preregistered (execution_manifest). Model calls used: 160 (one shared initial generation per task); no technical failures affecting confirmatory outcomes. Confirmatory numeric summary (artifact‑backed): N=160 paired tasks; baseline actionable = 0/160; guarded actionable = 0/160; contingency: n11=160, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (A−C)=0.00. Bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729): [0.00,0.00]. McNemar exact two‑sided p=1.00. Validator operational summary (artifact references): across the 160 confirmatory episodes, the guarded validator did not produce blocking events that changed the simulator’s enacted actionable label (blocked count on confirmatory set = 0 as reflected in the contingency n10/n01=0 and the per‑task scoring artifacts under execution/scoring/*.json; see execution_manifest.artifact_hashes and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). All principal numbers and tests reported here match the analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and the artifact hashes recorded in the execution manifest).
sections.discussion: The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (≥30% relative reduction) cannot be evaluated because the baseline actionable proportion was zero. In other words, the planned relative‑reduction target is undefined when baseline=0; the null/degenerate outcome is a ceiling effect rather than evidence of equivalence. Possible interpretable causes supported by the archived traces: (1) task difficulty calibration — the confirmatory task set produced generation outputs that the simulator judged non‑actionable under its formal safety predicate; (2) narrowness of simulator safety predicate — the deterministic checks capture a specific class of actionable faults and may not reflect all operational hazards (construct validity threat); (3) single‑model scope — results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the supplied prompt and cannot generalize across model families or prompt variants. Operational implication: a guarded pipeline can only reduce enactable faults when baseline generation produces enactable faults detectable by the chosen validator/simulator; when baseline is already safe under the chosen predicate, the pipeline yields no measurable reduction. We therefore recommend for future confirmatory work: (i) harder, adversarialized task sets and calibrated positive baseline rates; (ii) multi‑model evaluation to test generality; (iii) multi‑validator scoring (richer simulator predicates or human‑in‑the‑loop adjudication) to widen construct validity. All raw traces are published for re‑scoring with alternative validators (execution/raw_results.jsonl; analysis artifacts and hashes are in the execution manifest).
sections.conclusion: We implemented a fully preregistered paired evaluation of a generate→validate→simulate→rollback pipeline versus generation‑only for LLM‑assisted NetOps using gpt‑5‑mini on 160 confirmatory tasks. Observed outcome: both conditions produced zero actionable misconfigurations under the deterministic simulator and safety checks (paired difference = 0.00, 95% CI [0.00,0.00], p=1.00). The preregistered relative‑reduction target is not evaluable due to baseline=0 (ceiling effect). The null result emphasises the need for appropriately calibrated task difficulty, multi‑model and multi‑validator protocols, and deployment‑realistic evaluation criteria to meaningfully measure pipeline benefits. We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, raw outputs, scoring files, and analysis artifacts so the community can re‑score or extend the study with harder tasks or alternative validators.

limitations: Confirmatory task set produced a ceiling effect (baseline generation judged non‑actionable by the simulator), preventing evaluation of the preregistered relative‑reduction target (≥30%).
Single model (gpt‑5‑mini) — results do not generalize to other foundation models or model sizes without additional runs.
Deterministic simulator safety predicate is an abstraction and may not capture all real‑world operational failure modes (construct validity).
Public/synthetic vendor‑neutral tasks; no live device enactment or production telemetry was used (external validity).
Potential residual contamination risk from overlap between public corpus and model training data was mitigated per preregistered hashing/similarity checks but cannot be fully excluded.
